newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers focus on money after Simpson verdict.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers focus on money after Simpson verdict.

text.p: Victorious plaintiffs focused on Wednesday on convincing a civil trial jury to slap O.J. Simpson with punitive damages on top of the $8.5 million he must pay in the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend.

A hearing between lawyers and Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki was scheduled in the Santa Monica courthouse where a predominantly white jury on Tuesday found the black former football star liable for the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.

The jury's unanimous verdict ordered him to pay $8.5 million in compensatory damages to Goldman's family. He could be slapped with millions more in punitive damages in the next phase of the trial set to begin on Thursday.
Simpson was acquitted of the murders in October 1995 by a mostly black criminal jury but was sued in civil court by the victims' families seeking monetary damages.

Once again, public reaction to a Simpson verdict was split sharply along racial lines. This time most whites said justice was served while most blacks called it unjust -- a reversal in the attitudes that prevailed after Simpson's criminal trial.

Plaintiffs' lawyers on Wednesday were mapping their strategy for Thursday's session when the jury will hear financial experts testifying on the ex-football star's net worth. Defence lawyers, who were forced last week to hand over details of Simpson's financial assets to the plaintiffs' legal team, were expected to try to block what the experts would tell the jury about his wealth.

Simpson will serve no jail time but could lose much of what is left of the fortune he earned in his days as a football star, advertising pitchman and sportscaster. Attorney Leo Terrell, a friend and strong supporter of Simpson, told Cable News Network the verdict would be appealed.
Attorney Robert Tourtelot, who filed suit on behalf of the Goldmans before being replaced, said the "huge" compensatory damages showed the punitive award "is going to be gigantic."

Simpson's net worth, estimated at $11 million four years ago, has been shrunk by legal costs and most of his remaining $3 million is sunk into untouchable pension and retirement funds, according to an investigation by CNN and Time magazine.
But legal analysts say the plaintiffs can hound him for the rest of his life, forcing him to auction off his Bentley, give up his tennis courts and adopt a more modest lifestyle.
While Goldman's family alone is entitled to the compensatory damages, Nicole Brown Simpson's estate will share in any punitive damages.

Harvard law professor Alan Dershowitz, an adviser to Simpson's criminal defence team, said there were "some very substantial issues" on which to base an appeal: "The admission of the lie-detector test evidence, the anonymous phone call to the battered women's hotline from a woman called Nicole ... and the manner by which the jury was selected."

But Dershowitz held out little chance of a reversal of the verdict. "Judges in California are going to look very long and hard before they reverse what will be a very popular verdict among their constituents. I don't predict there will be a reversal of this verdict," he told NBC's "Today" show.

Christopher Darden, a member of the unsuccessful criminal trial prosecution team, said the difference in the civil case was that Simpson had to testify. "O.J. lied in front of this jury, he lied to the black community and he lied to the American public. This jury focused on the evidence, not race or politics," he said.

Simpson, booed and jeered as he left the courthouse on Tuesday, could face a problem more personal than his finances. A domestic violence prevention group called on Wednesday for a family court to reconsider awarding him custody of the two young children he had with his slain ex-wife. The children lived with the Brown family after Simpson's 1994 arrest and were returned to him just before Christmas.

"Now that a jury has found O.J. Simpson responsible for the brutal murders of the ex-wife he had battered ... California courts should quickly reconsider ..." the San Francisco-based Family Violence Prevention Fund said.
